Publications were further analyzed based on relevance, subject focus, and type of study. After a further round of selection, the sample was reduced to about only 100 articles, and 44 of these were identified as the most relevant for detailed analysis.

The initial search strategy yielded more than 3,000 publications related broadly to artificial intelligence (AI). However, a substantial share of these studies addressed AI from a purely technical, computational, or engineering perspective without explicit relevance to labour market outcomes, employment structures, or human resource management. Given the interdisciplinary nature of AI research, an additional thematic delimitation step was therefore required to systematically identify studies situated at the intersection of AI and labour market analysis.

To achieve this, we employed VOSviewer (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#Fig3)), a bibliometric visualisation tool, to conduct a co-occurrence analysis of keywords based on titles, abstracts, and author keywords. This approach allowed us to map the conceptual structure of the AI-related literature and to distinguish clusters focusing on labour market, employment, skills, human resources, and organisational change from those centred on algorithmic development or technical optimisation.

**Fig. 3**

Analysis of scientific papers with VOSviewer

The co-occurrence network was constructed using VOSviewer based on keyword extraction from titles, abstracts, and author keywords. A minimum occurrence threshold of five was applied to reduce noise in the network. The full counting method was used for co-occurrence calculation, and association strength normalization was applied for link weighting. The clustering structure was generated using the default VOSviewer modularity-based clustering algorithm.

Specifically, keywords such as _labour market_, _employment_, _jobs_, _skills_, _human resources_, _wages_, and _workplace_ were used as focal points in the co-occurrence network. Publications located within or closely connected to these thematic clusters were retained for further screening, while studies positioned exclusively within technical AI clusters were excluded. This bibliometric filtering step substantially reduced the dataset to a thematically coherent subset of publications with direct relevance to the research problem.

Following this visual and thematic delimitation, the remaining publications were subjected to manual screening based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria and assessed using a modified PRISMA 2020 framework. This two-step process—combining bibliometric mapping with qualitative screening—ensured that the final sample captured the most relevant scholarly contributions addressing the impact of AI on labour market dynamics rather than AI development in general.

As we can see, at first glance it may seem that the issue of AI’s impact on the labour market has been extensively studied and analysed. However, this is not the case; in fact, there are very few scholarly research papers that have addressed this issue. This research aims to understand the recent impact of AI (analysed through analysis using WoS and PRISMA 2020 standard) on different aspects of the implementation of AI in the labour market and identify the primary challenges that limit its broader adoption.

The implementation of AI in HR management represents one of the strongest positive significant transformations of the current labour market. Despite the obvious benefits of AI, such as decision support, turnover prediction, or optimization of HR processes, its implementation raises serious questions about employment equity, disproportional distribution of benefits, gender and skill inequalities, and different approaches to employee retraining and participation. An important factor influencing the impact of AI is the institutional environment and the ability of organisations to involve employees in co-creating technological change.

Despite the abundance of scholarly literature and scientific papers, both in journals and at conferences, on the economic and technological aspects of AI, a comprehensive overview of how AI adoption affects job seekers, workers themselves, and interpersonal employment relationships, as well as skill dynamics across sectors, is lacking. Most existing studies rely on the rationale of technological progress, while overlooking the social, participatory, and institutional dimensions of AI implementation. This study responds to this gap by examining how AI adoption works from an interdisciplinary perspective, with an emphasis on technological, organizational, and human aspects.

### 2.1 Research problem

_How does the implementation of AI influence job structures_,_skill requirements_,_and equity in employment across sectors and organisations with different levels of technological maturity and institutional capacity?_

The proposed research aims to explore how the impacts of implementing AI in HR vary between sectors and different types of organisations, with a focus on changes in employment, skills requirements and perceptions of fairness. The research will be based on a holistic approach that includes technological, organisational, institutional, and social aspects of AI implementation. This framework will identify the key factors that determine whether AI contributes to an inclusive transformation of the working environment or, on the other hand, leads to an increase in existing inequalities.

Based on the research problem, we set the research questions. Each of the proposed research questions addresses a critical aspect of how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms the labour market. Together, they provide a comprehensive lens for analysing the structural, organisational, and human-level implications of AI adoption.

RQ1: How are skill requirements evolving as a result of AI adoption in different sectors?

This question aims to identify the specific changes in the demand for skills driven by AI, such as the increasing importance of technical, data-analytical, and soft skills, and the obsolescence of certain routine competencies. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing responsive training programmes, shaping educational curricula, and supporting workforce adaptability.

### Contribution RQ1

Offers insights for policymakers and educational institutions to anticipate future skill needs and align learning pathways accordingly.

RQ2: To what extent does AI contribute to employment polarisation between high- and low-skilled workers?

This question explores whether AI accelerates the divergence in employment opportunities and earnings between highly skilled and low-skilled workers. It addresses the concern that AI may disproportionately benefit those already in advantaged labour market positions, thereby reinforcing existing inequalities.

### Contribution RQ2

Provides empirical evidence to inform equity-oriented labour market policies and contributes to the theoretical discourse on skill-biased technological change.

RQ3: How does the institutional environment affect the implementation and outcomes of AI in the workplace?

This question investigates the role of institutions—such as trade unions, legal frameworks, and participatory decision-making structures—in mediating the effects of AI. The institutional context can either amplify or mitigate the risks of job displacement, inequality, and algorithmic control.

### Contribution RQ3

Highlights the importance of social governance and participatory practices, offering guidance for inclusive digital transformation strategies.

RQ4: What strategies are companies using to address skill gaps and facilitate reskilling in the context of AI?

This question examines how organisations respond to AI-induced skill shortages—whether through investment in employee training, hiring strategies, or partnerships with educational providers. It sheds light on organisational readiness and capacity to adapt to technological change.

### Contribution RQ4

Informs human resource development practices and fosters understanding of effective approaches to reskilling and workforce sustainability.

RQ5: To what extent does AI implementation result in job displacement versus the creation of new roles?

This question assesses the balance between automation-driven job loss and the emergence of new positions requiring novel competencies. It aims to clarify the extent to which AI disrupts employment or facilitates occupational transformation and innovation.

### Contribution RQ5

Supports a more nuanced view of “technological unemployment” and provides data for forecasting future employment trends in the context of digital transformation.

### 2.2 Analytical propositions guiding the thematic synthesis

Based on the research problem and research questions, this study formulates a set of analytical propositions that serve as organising devices for the thematic synthesis of the reviewed literature. These propositions are not hypotheses in the confirmatory sense, nor are they empirically tested within this study. Instead, they provide a structured lens through which convergence, divergence, and contextual variation across existing studies can be systematically examined. This approach is consistent with qualitative and integrative literature review methodologies, where propositions are used to guide interpretation rather than to validate causal claims.

### AP1

Employee participation and job insecurity.

*   _Rationale_: Employee participation and voice have long been recognised as central mechanisms shaping employee perceptions during periods of organisational and technological change trust (Doellgast, [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR17 "Doellgast, V.                   https://doi.org/10.1080/10301763.2022.2111987
                  
                ")). Recent contributions in the context of AI adoption highlight participation as a potential moderator of employee responses, including perceived job insecurity and acceptance of algorithmic management (Gómez Gandía et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR20 "Gómez Gandía, J. A., Gavrila, G., de Lucas Ancillo, S., A., & del Val Núñez, M. T. (2025).                   https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techfore.2024.123908
                  
                ")). These strands of literature provide the conceptual grounding for treating employee participation as a key analytical dimension in the synthesis.

*   _Analytical focus_: The synthesis examines how the reviewed studies conceptualise employee participation in AI-related decision-making and how they discuss its relationship with perceived job insecurity and related employee outcomes across different organisational and institutional contexts.

## 3 Literature review

In the literature review, we describe various approaches that are currently implemented as AI elements in the labour market. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a broad field that encompasses different computational approaches designed to perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, or decision-making. Within AI, machine learning (ML) has become the most influential subfield, as it allows algorithms to improve their performance through exposure to data rather than explicit programming. Building on ML, a number of specialised application areas have emerged that are particularly relevant to the labour market and human resource management, such as Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Recommender Systems (RS). These methods can be very effective as an initial filter when submitting applications / CVs of applicants to larger companies, or for quickly determining the correctness of code for programmers.

### 3.1 Machine learning

For example, a study in China applied deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to predict mineralization potential in gold deposits, illustrating how ML can manage complex, high-dimensional datasets and make accurate predictions in uncertain environments. The dataset included 43 features per spatial unit, comprising 39 geochemical elements (such as Ag, Au, Pb, Zn) and 4 geological features (faults and stratigraphic layers), with data density of 4 samples/km². The data were split into training and testing areas at an 8:2 ratio to evaluate model performance. The DRL agent treated each data point as a state and interacted with the environment to predict high or low mineralization potential. The model used ε-greedy policy and replay memory, with neural networks having three hidden layers (256, 64, 16 units). During training, the agent gradually learned to distinguish between known deposits and unlabeled areas. In the testing area, approximately 48.94% of the mineral potential areas identified by DRL with optimal parameters (_n_ = 0.8, _p_ = 0.2) contained around 80% of known gold deposits, while about 60% of these predicted areas covered 100% of known deposits, demonstrating strong predictive power. This example highlights that ML models, when properly designed, can leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to predict complex outcomes, even in dynamic or poorly understood systems. Similarly, in the labour market, predictive models trained on employee datasets (e.g., demographics, performance metrics, tenure) can forecast turnover probabilities, optimise staffing plans, and identify employees at risk of leaving, thereby improving workforce stability. The success metrics in these studies—such as the proportion of correctly identified deposits—are analogous to measures like prediction accuracy, recall, or precision in HR analytics, showing the tangible impact of AI-driven predictions. (Shi et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR38 "Shi, Z., Zuo, R., & Zhou, B. (2023). Deep Reinforcement Learning for Mineral Prospectivity Mapping. Mathematical Geosciences, 55(6), 773–797. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11004-023-10059-9
                  
                ")). ML thus provides the methodological foundation on which more specialised applications, such as NLP or RS, can be built. Machine learning thus provides the foundation for specialised applications such as NLP or recommender systems. In health data, models like random forests, SVMs, and neural networks are evaluated using metrics such as AUC, F₁-score, and recall. High AUC values (closer to 1.0) indicate strong predictive ability, while 0.5 corresponds to random performance. These metrics allow ML to handle high-dimensional datasets like EHRs or genomic data and quantify predictive performance objectively. (Cho et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR13 "Cho, H., She, J., De Marchi, D., El-Zaatari, H., Barnes, E. L., Kahkoska, A. R., Kosorok, M. R., & Virkud, A. V. (2024). Machine Learning and Health Science Research: Tutorial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 26, e50890. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2196/50890
                  
                ")).

### 3.2 Natural Language Processing

Natural Language Processing (NLP) applies ML algorithms to textual and spoken data to understand, classify, or generate human language. Key HR applications include CV screening, employee feedback analysis, and sentiment monitoring. Modern NLP relies on pre-trained deep learning models, especially BERT and GPT variants, which achieve over 90% accuracy on benchmark tasks like sentiment analysis (IMDB: 50,000 reviews) and question answering (SQuAD-1.1: 100,000 questions; SQuAD-2.0: 150,000 questions including unanswerable ones). These models use large unlabeled corpora for pre-training and fine-tuning on target datasets, exploiting architectures such as transformers with self-attention, which outperform classical ML methods and RNNs. For instance, GPT-2 (1.5B parameters) and GPT-3 (175B parameters) generate human-like text and enable zero- and few-shot learning. Despite their high performance, challenges remain in computational cost, interpretability, and reproducibility, as only 26% of recent papers report multiple fine-tuning runs, and 80% lack complete model selection procedures (Lauriola et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR28 "Lauriola, I., Lavelli, A., & Aiolli, F. (2022). An introduction to Deep Learning in Natural Language Processing: Models, techniques, and tools. Neurocomputing, 470, 443–456. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2021.05.103
                  
                ")). Beyond traditional NLP tasks, these techniques have also been successfully applied to predictive optimization problems, where a study evaluated four vectorization and seven regression techniques to forecast application performance. Using NLP to analyze the input code, the framework predicts the optimal optimization sequence with a minimum performance drop of 0.5% and an average drop of 18% compared to the actual best sequence, demonstrating the ability of NLP-driven methods to identify highly accurate, task-specific solutions and highlighting their practical relevance for HR and other domain-specific applications (Ahmed et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR1 "Ahmed, H., Fahim Ul Haque, M., Raza Khan, H., Nadeem, G., Arshad, K., Assaleh, K., & Cesar Santos, P. (2024). Selecting the Best Compiler Optimization by Adopting Natural Language Processing. Ieee Access : Practical Innovations, Open Solutions, 12, 121700–121711. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3451516
                  
                ")).

### 3.3 Recommender Systems

Recommender Systems (RS) represent another major application area that builds directly on ML techniques. Unlike NLP, which focuses on language, RS use data on user preferences and behaviour to generate personalised recommendations. In the HR context, this includes suggesting suitable candidates for a vacancy, recommending training opportunities, or mapping career development paths. Experimental studies on movie recommendation datasets, such as MovieLens 100k and IMDB, demonstrate that combining PCA feature extraction, K-means clustering, and collaborative filtering yields highly accurate recommendations. For instance, clustering movies into six groups based on genre and incorporating user demographic attributes enabled the system to predict relevant items efficiently, achieving strong precision, recall, and F-measure scores while reducing runtime. These results highlight how RS can leverage ML techniques to generate targeted, high-quality recommendations, showing potential for analogous applications in HR decision-making (Yassine et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR46 "Yassine, A., Mohamed, L., & Al Achhab, M. (2021). Intelligent recommender system based on unsupervised machine learning and demographic attributes. Simulation Modelling Practice and Theory, 107, 102198. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.simpat.2020.102198
                  
                ")). Modern RS combine collaborative filtering with content-based and hybrid approaches, often supported by deep learning. Although RS are technically an application of ML rather than a distinct conceptual field, they illustrate how AI can be operationalised in human resource management to improve decision-making and employee development.

### 3.4 AI in relation to the labour market

This section synthesises the reviewed studies thematically to highlight shared patterns and divergences in the literature, rather than presenting isolated study-by-study summaries. The findings are grouped into interconnected sub-themes reflecting key labour market dynamics associated with AI adoption. Empirical research using quantitative surveys with 420 responses (210 from business leaders, 210 from employees) shows statistically significant differences in the perception of automation across four areas: Business Processes, Technology and Tools, Skills and Professional Development, and Motivation and Engagement. For example, regarding workflow simplification (A1), business leaders rated it positively with a mean of 4.19 (SD = 0.394), while employees rated it 4.03 (SD = 0.167, t(210) = 5487, _p_< 0.05, d = 0.54). Similarly, in Technology and Tools, business leaders saw higher benefits in tools efficiency (B1, M = 3.66, SD = 0.476) compared to employees (M = 3.20, SD = 0.401, t(210) = 10.647, _p_< 0.05, d = 1.04). Differences were also notable in Skills and Professional Development, with work-life balance (C3) rated much lower by employees (M = 2.26, SD = 0.441) than by business leaders (M = 2.99, SD = 0.138, t(210) = 22.861, _p_< 0.05, d = 2.23). Across Motivation and Engagement, large differences were observed in creativity (D1, d = 0.93), career planning (D2, d = 0.82), and skill obsolescence (D5, d = 0.8). These results illustrate that while management emphasises efficiency and operational gains, employees are more concerned about job security, skill requirements, and personal development. Such divergent perspectives underline that AI adoption is not solely a technical process but also a socio-organisational one. Sustainable implementation, therefore requires participatory approaches, transparent communication, and targeted investment in competence development to align organisational objectives with employee needs and support long-term workforce sustainability (Gómez Gandía et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR20 "Gómez Gandía, J. A., Gavrila, G., de Lucas Ancillo, S., A., & del Val Núñez, M. T. (2025). Towards sustainable business in the automation era: Exploring its transformative impact from top management and employee perspective. Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 210, 123908. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techfore.2024.123908
                  
                ")).

#### 3.4.1 AI, human work, and organizational processes

Social skills are a key element of the added value of human work, as they enable effective collaboration, strengthen relationship networks, and contribute to productivity and salary growth. Evidence from the dataset on the joint use of AI and human resources (HR) demonstrates this clearly: even when AI and HR prices were equal, a minimum of 25% of daily labor hours was still required for AI to operate effectively. AI was able to reduce the remaining labor hours by approximately 50%, but the hours saved were not eliminated; instead, they were redeployed across other segments of work to maintain speed and quality. For example, for laborers with wage rates around $124.50 per hour, 32 h of work per day were initially required, but after partial AI integration, 12 h were saved and reinvested into complementary tasks, while the total AI service bill matched the value of the saved labor hours. These findings confirm that AI primarily serves as a complement rather than a replacement for human labor: it accelerates task completion and reduces repetitive effort, but cannot replicate the nuanced judgment, adaptability, and social skills that humans provide (Das, [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR16 "Das, D. (2023). Understanding the choice of human resource and the artificial intelligence: strategic behavior and the existence of industry equilibrium. Journal of Economic Studies, 50(2), 234–267. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/JES-06-2021-0305
                  
                ")). Integrating AI in HR improves efficiency and accuracy of decision-making through data-driven processes. AI tools such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and chatbots optimize workforce planning, talent management, performance reviews, and training. This transformation allows HR departments to focus on strategic activities while reducing the cost and time associated with routine administrative tasks (Benabou & Touhami, [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR7 "Benabou, A., & Touhami, F. (2025). Empowering human resource management through artificial intelligence: A systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis. International Journal of Production Management and Engineering, 13(1), 59–76. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4995/ijpme.2025.21900
                  
                ")). Chatbots are a modern HR tool that makes the recruitment process, communication, and administrative tasks easier and more efficient. They automate answering frequently asked questions, scheduling meetings, and collecting feedback, which evidence suggests reduces the workload of the HR department and enables consistent communication between candidates, employees, and recruiters. Implementing chatbots also transforms the way HR departments operate by allowing them to focus on strategic activities such as employee development and building a strong employee culture. Modern HR chatbots use artificial intelligence and machine learning to automate routine processes, increasing efficiency and reducing errors, although they still face the challenges of answering complex queries and the need for regular maintenance (Majumder & Mondal, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR31 "Majumder, S., & Mondal, A. (2021). Are chatbots really useful for human resource management? International Journal of Speech Technology, 24(4), 969–977. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10772-021-09834-y
                  
                ")). While tools such as chatbots illustrate the operational integration of AI into HR processes, the broader economic implications of AI adoption depend strongly on how these technologies are priced and deployed within organisational decision-making frameworks.

Therefore although AI integration can significantly increase productivity and streamline decision-making processes, its ability to fully replace human labour is limited by several factors. These include the availability of data that may be incomplete or incorrect, technical limitations of current AI systems, and market conditions that affect the cost and effectiveness of automation. According to (Das, [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR16 "Das, D. (2023). Understanding the choice of human resource and the artificial intelligence: strategic behavior and the existence of industry equilibrium. Journal of Economic Studies, 50(2), 234–267. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/JES-06-2021-0305
                  
                ")) in linear pricing there is mass adoption of AI, which allows HR and AI to substitute for each other, while in the non-convex case, where AI is priced non-linearly, the innovator gains some monopoly share and there is complementarity between HR and AI. Overall industry demand is furthermore strongly influenced by the company with the highest preference for AI, showing how strategic decision-making and budget constraints shape substitution and complementarity between HR and AI technologies.

At an individual level, AI improves employee satisfaction, engagement, and overall performance by automating routine administrative tasks and freeing time for strategic activities. Empirical studies across 24 countries and 297 firms show that AI-enabled HRM applications provide personalized support, enhance learning, and reduce turnover, while technological competence and firm-specific factors significantly influence AI adoption. From a business perspective, AI adoption leads to higher productivity, lower costs, and more efficient processes, boosting competitiveness. However, evidence also highlights risks such as increased uncertainty, stress, and the potential threat of human labour substitution.

Beyond organisational efficiency, the adoption of AI also affects employees directly at the individual level, influencing satisfaction, engagement, and perceived job security. Effective change management, socio-technical interventions, and AI-human configurations are therefore critical to balance efficiency gains with employee well-being and ensure positive organisational outcomes (Budhwar et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR10 "Budhwar, P., Malik, A., De Silva, M. T. T., & Thevisuthan, P. (2022). Artificial intelligence – challenges and opportunities for international HRM: a review and research agenda. The International Journal of Human Resource Management, 33(6), 1065–1097. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/09585192.2022.2035161
                  
                ")). Introducing technologies such as AI and robotics into HR brings greater efficiency and personalisation to processes such as recruitment, training and performance reviews. At the same time, it raises concerns about privacy, over-supervision and a decrease in employee motivation (Shahid et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR36 "Shahid, S., Kaur, K., Mohyuddin, S. M., Prikshat, V., & Patel, P. (2025). Revolutionizing HRM: a review of human-robot collaboration in HRM functions and the imperative of change readiness. Business Process Management Journal. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/BPMJ-12-2023-0951
                  
                ")). The implementation of AI in companies leads to higher labour cost inertia, suggesting that AI augments workers’ capabilities rather than replaces them. As a result, companies rely more on skilled workers, which increases the costs associated with their adjustment and adaptation. To benefit from this change, companies should encourage continuous learning and adapt work processes so that both people and AI work effectively together. For example study analysed 28.463 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed nonfinancial firms from 2006 to 2020, using a textual measure of AI adoption based on annual reports. On average, firms mention 0.781 AI-related words per 1000 words, reflecting heterogeneous adoption across industries and time, with higher adoption in high-tech, IT, and capital-intensive sectors. Empirical results show that AI adoption significantly increases labor cost stickiness, indicating that AI tends to augment rather than replace employees, particularly in firms with higher-skilled workers, capital-intensive operations, and regions with older populations (H. Wang & Qiu, [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR44 "Wang, H., & Qiu, F. (2023). AI adoption and labor cost stickiness: based on natural language and machine learning. Information Technology and Management. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10799-023-00408-9
                  
                ")). Digitisation and the expansion of AI are fundamentally changing the nature of work processes, especially in areas that have traditionally been seen as the domain of human creativity. Research indicates that instead of replacing human labour completely, it becomes reorganised. The automation of routine or technically specific tasks is changing the skill requirements of employees, reinforcing the importance of technological and data-analytical skills, while increasing the need for adaptive and interdisciplinary thinking For example the study (Akmeraner-Kökat & Pellandini-Simányi, [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR2 "Akmeraner-Kökat, Y., & Pellandini-Simányi, L. (2025). Creativity re-distributed: how digitalisation changes creative advertising practice. Journal of Marketing Management, 1–23. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/0267257X.2025.2467299
                  
                ")), was based on a qualitative case analysis of a data-driven creative agency in Türkiye, drawing on 35 semi-structured in-depth interviews with copywriters, art directors, data analysts, and marketing specialists, complemented by pilot interviews and industry media analysis. Using purposive and snowball sampling, the research examines how digitalisation and AI reshape creative advertising work practices. The study documents the widespread use of A/B/C testing, where alternative designs are exposed to samples of approximately 1,000 users, and selection is based on click-through and engagement rates. Metrics such as impressions, engagement and conversion rates increasingly govern creative decisions, shifting creatives’ roles towards managing and responding to quantified feedback. Overall, the results show that AI does not replace human creativity but redistributes it, embedding human ideas into modular, data-driven systems that prioritise efficiency, scalability and measurable performance over artistic autonomy (Akmeraner-Kökat & Pellandini-Simányi, [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR2 "Akmeraner-Kökat, Y., & Pellandini-Simányi, L. (2025). Creativity re-distributed: how digitalisation changes creative advertising practice. Journal of Marketing Management, 1–23. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/0267257X.2025.2467299
                  
                ")).

While these organisational transformations reshape internal work processes, they also raise broader questions about employment dynamics, including job creation, displacement, and sectoral differences.

#### 3.4.2 Employment effects: job creation, displacement, and sectoral differences

The deployment of AI not only improves productivity and the quality of work processes, but also raises questions about ethics, transparency, and potential job displacement (Aly, [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR4 "Aly, H. (2022). Digital transformation, development and productivity in developing countries: is artificial intelligence a curse or a blessing? Review of Economics and Political Science, 7(4), 238–256. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/REPS-11-2019-0145
                  
                ")). Econometric estimations confirm that digital transformation has a positive impact not only on economic development and labour productivity, but also on the overall employment rate. An interesting finding is that this positive effect is strongly reflected in female employment, suggesting that digitalisation may contribute to reducing gender inequality in the labour market. On the other hand, the effect of digital transformation on vulnerable employment is not found to be significant, suggesting that the reduction of vulnerable jobs depends more on other socio-economic and legal measures (Aly, [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR4 "Aly, H. (2022). Digital transformation, development and productivity in developing countries: is artificial intelligence a curse or a blessing? Review of Economics and Political Science, 7(4), 238–256. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/REPS-11-2019-0145
                  
                ")). The empirical analysis of 25 developing countries (2017) shows that digital transformation, measured by the Digital Evolution Index (DEI), is strongly and significantly associated with higher labor productivity and economic development. Specifically, a one-unit increase in DEI is linked to an increase of approximately USD 19,000 in labor productivity and a 1.3–1.45 rise in log per capita GNI, confirming productivity-driven growth effects. While descriptive evidence shows no clear unconditional relationship with employment, econometric results (FGLS) reveal a statistically significant positive impact of digital transformation on total employment, driven mainly by higher female employment. In contrast, no significant relationship is found between digital transformation and vulnerable employment, suggesting that technology alone does not improve job quality without supportive labor institutions. Overall, the results highlight that digital transformation enhances efficiency and growth, but its social outcomes depend on complementary policies and change management (Aly, [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR4 "Aly, H. (2022). Digital transformation, development and productivity in developing countries: is artificial intelligence a curse or a blessing? Review of Economics and Political Science, 7(4), 238–256. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/REPS-11-2019-0145
                  
                ")).

In 2017, only 5.8% of U.S. companies used AI. However, when weighted by the number of employees, the adoption rate rises to 18.2% (see Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#Fig4)). This indicates that AI use is concentrated in large enterprises and fast-growing start-ups. The low average penetration rate suggests the existence of significant barriers and obstacles to AI adoption, which large enterprises have been able to overcome due to their size, thereby consolidating their competitive advantages. Analysis of start-ups reveals a strong association between AI use and process innovation, suggesting that innovative firms with high growth potential can drive the wider adoption of AI. Failure to tackle the current unequal tempo of AI adoption may result in increasing gaps in productivity, remuneration and career opportunities between tech-mature companies and small or less digitally mature businesses (McElheran et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR32 "McElheran, K., Li, J. F., Brynjolfsson, E., Kroff, Z., Dinlersoz, E., Foster, L., & Zolas, N. (2024). AI adoption in America: Who, what, and where. Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, 33(2), 375–415. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/jems.12576
                  
                ")).

**Fig. 4**

AI adoption rate (McElheran et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#ref-CR32 "McElheran, K., Li, J. F., Brynjolfsson, E., Kroff, Z., Dinlersoz, E., Foster, L., & Zolas, N. (2024). AI adoption in America: Who, what, and where. Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, 33(2), 375–415. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/jems.12576
                  
                "))

Differences in the intensity of AI use across sectors suggest that the impact of this technology on the labour market will be very strong. As shown in Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44491-026-00003-y#Fig5), the highest intensity of AI use is observed in the information, healthcare and manufacturing sectors, where the proportion of companies with high intensity of AI use is greatest.

In contrast, sectors such as retail, transport, construction, or agriculture show overall lower adoption of these technologies. This difference is a result of the varying technological readiness, innovation capacity in each sector, and the specific character of the work they do. At the same time, it means that the impacts of AI on employment, skills requirements, and inequalities will largely depend on the context of the specific sector.

**Fig. 5**
